blocks.en: 📖 Deacon Family Ministry Plan — Unit 6: Ongoing Care — Visitation and Prayer
blocks.es_reference: 📖 Plan de Ministerio Familiar del Diácono — Unidad 6: Cuidado Continuo — Visitación y Oración

blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "Pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their trouble..." — James 1:27 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: «La religión pura y sin mácula delante de Dios y Padre es esta: Visitar a los huérfanos y a las viudas en sus tribulaciones...» — Santiago 1:27 (RVG)

blocks.en: In Unit 5 the families were assigned and introduced. The deacon has met the families given to him, and the relationship has begun. But an introduction is only a beginning. Now comes the work that makes the Plan more than a paper arrangement — the ongoing, year-round ministry by which the deacon actually cares for the families entrusted to him. That ongoing care flows mainly through two channels: the deacon goes to his families, and he prays for them.
blocks.es_reference: En la Unidad 5 las familias fueron asignadas y presentadas. El diácono ha conocido a las familias que le fueron dadas, y la relación ha comenzado. Pero una presentación es solo un comienzo. Ahora viene la obra que hace del Plan algo más que un arreglo en el papel — el ministerio continuo, de todo el año, por el cual el diácono de veras cuida de las familias que se le confían. Ese cuidado continuo fluye principalmente por dos canales: el diácono va a sus familias, y ora por ellas.

blocks.en: Why must the care be ongoing? Because care that arrives only in a crisis is too little and too late. The relationship must be kept alive between the troubles, so that when trouble finally comes the deacon is already a trusted friend and not a stranger knocking at the door. Pure religion, James tells us, visits the widow and the orphan in their trouble — and it is the deacon who has visited all along who will be welcome when the trouble comes.
blocks.es_reference: ¿Por qué debe ser continuo el cuidado? Porque el cuidado que llega solo en una crisis es demasiado poco y demasiado tarde. La relación debe mantenerse viva entre las dificultades, de modo que cuando por fin venga la dificultad el diácono sea ya un amigo de confianza y no un extraño que toca a la puerta. La religión pura, nos dice Santiago, visita a la viuda y al huérfano en su tribulación — y es el diácono que ha visitado todo el tiempo el que será bienvenido cuando venga la dificultad.

blocks.en: Subject: the ongoing care of the deacon for his families.
blocks.es_reference: Tema: el cuidado continuo del diácono por sus familias.

blocks.en: Proposition: The deacon cares for his families continually through two great ministries — the ministry of visitation, by which he goes to them, and the ministry of prayer, by which he carries them to God — and he sustains both by faithfulness through the years.
blocks.es_reference: Proposición: El diácono cuida de sus familias continuamente por medio de dos grandes ministerios — el ministerio de la visitación, por el cual va a ellas, y el ministerio de la oración, por el cual las lleva a Dios — y sostiene ambos por la fidelidad a través de los años.

blocks.en: We take up, then, these two ministries, and the faithfulness that holds them up.
blocks.es_reference: Tomamos, pues, estos dos ministerios, y la fidelidad que los sostiene.

blocks.en: I. The Ministry of Visitation: Why the Deacon Goes
blocks.es_reference: I. El Ministerio de la Visitación: Por Qué Va el Diácono

blocks.en: The first and most visible work of ongoing care is visitation — going to the people where they are. This is no mere church custom; it runs deep in Scripture. James makes it the very heart of pure religion: to visit the orphan and the widow in their trouble. And the Lord Himself makes visiting the sick and the imprisoned a mark of true love for Him.
blocks.es_reference: La primera y más visible obra del cuidado continuo es la visitación — ir a las personas donde están. Esto no es una mera costumbre de iglesia; corre profundo en la Escritura. Santiago la hace el corazón mismo de la religión pura: visitar al huérfano y a la viuda en su tribulación. Y el Señor mismo hace del visitar al enfermo y al preso una marca del verdadero amor por Él.

blocks.en: I was naked and you clothed Me; I was sick and you visited Me; I was in prison and you came to Me... Assuredly, I say to you, inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these My brethren, you did it to Me. (Matthew 25:36, 40, NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: Estuve desnudo, y me cubristeis; enfermo, y me visitasteis; estuve en la cárcel, y vinisteis a mí... De cierto os digo que en cuanto lo hicisteis a uno de estos mis hermanos más pequeños, a mí lo hicisteis. (Mateo 25:36, 40, RVG)

blocks.en: To visit the least is to minister to Christ Himself. This was also the apostolic pattern, for Paul taught not only publicly but “from house to house” (Acts 20:20); the gospel goes to where people actually live. And there is something deeply fitting about going in person, for it follows the way of God Himself. He did not merely send a message from heaven; He sent His Son to dwell among us. A card is kind and a telephone call is good, but to show up — to be present in the living room, at the hospital bed, in the funeral home — embodies the love of Christ as nothing else can. The deacon goes because his Lord went.
blocks.es_reference: Visitar al más pequeño es ministrar a Cristo mismo. Este fue también el patrón apostólico, porque Pablo enseñó no solo públicamente sino «por las casas» (Hechos 20:20); el evangelio va a donde la gente realmente vive. Y hay algo profundamente apropiado en ir en persona, porque sigue el camino de Dios mismo. Él no se contentó con enviar un mensaje desde el cielo; envió a su Hijo para morar entre nosotros. Una tarjeta es amable y una llamada telefónica es buena, pero presentarse — estar presente en la sala, junto a la cama del hospital, en la funeraria — encarna el amor de Cristo como ninguna otra cosa puede. El diácono va porque su Señor fue.

blocks.en: Nor should the deacon ever underestimate what a single visit can do. To a person lying ill and afraid, to a widow sitting alone in a quiet house, to a family stunned by sudden loss, the knock at the door that says ‘the church has not forgotten you’ can be a lifeline. People remember for years the deacon who came when they were low. The visit preaches a sermon no pulpit can: that they are loved, that they belong, and that they are not alone.
blocks.es_reference: Tampoco debería el diácono jamás subestimar lo que una sola visita puede hacer. Para una persona enferma y temerosa, para una viuda sentada sola en una casa callada, para una familia aturdida por una pérdida repentina, el golpe en la puerta que dice «la iglesia no te ha olvidado» puede ser una cuerda de salvamento. La gente recuerda por años al diácono que vino cuando estaban abatidos. La visita predica un sermón que ningún púlpito puede: que son amados, que pertenecen, y que no están solos.

blocks.en: II. The Ministry of Visitation: Whom He Visits, and How Often
blocks.es_reference: II. El Ministerio de la Visitación: A Quién Visita, y Con Cuánta Frecuencia

blocks.en: Whom does the deacon visit? In one sense, all of his families. The whole point of the Plan is that every family has ongoing contact, not merely the few who speak up, so the deacon keeps in regular touch with each one, that none be forgotten. Yet certain people need special and prompt attention.
blocks.es_reference: ¿A quién visita el diácono? En un sentido, a todas sus familias. Todo el propósito del Plan es que cada familia tenga contacto continuo, no meramente los pocos que hablan, así que el diácono mantiene contacto regular con cada una, para que ninguna sea olvidada. Sin embargo, ciertas personas necesitan atención especial y pronta.

blocks.en: He goes to the sick and the shut-in, for those who cannot come to the church need the church to come to them — in the hospital, the nursing home, or the house they can no longer leave. He goes to the bereaved, who need a steady presence in their grief. He goes to the absent and the drifting, with a visit before the back door quietly closes. He goes to the new and the lonely — the newcomer to be welcomed, the widow or the single person easily overlooked. And he goes in times of joy as well: a new baby, a graduation, a milestone, for the deacon is to rejoice with those who rejoice and not only weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15).
blocks.es_reference: Va a los enfermos y los recluidos, porque los que no pueden venir a la iglesia necesitan que la iglesia venga a ellos — en el hospital, el asilo, o la casa que ya no pueden dejar. Va a los afligidos, que necesitan una presencia constante en su dolor. Va a los ausentes y los que se alejan, con una visita antes de que la puerta trasera se cierre calladamente. Va a los nuevos y los solitarios — el recién llegado que ha de ser recibido, la viuda o la persona sola fácilmente pasada por alto. Y va también en tiempos de gozo: un nuevo bebé, una graduación, un hito, porque el diácono ha de gozarse con los que se gozan y no solo llorar con los que lloran (Romanos 12:15).

blocks.en: How often does he go? Regularly enough that the relationship stays alive. The exact rhythm will vary from family to family, but the principle is steady, ongoing contact — not a single visit at the start followed by years of silence. A faithful deacon's families hear from him through the year, in good seasons and bad, so that he is always near at hand.
blocks.es_reference: ¿Con cuánta frecuencia va? Lo suficiente para que la relación se mantenga viva. El ritmo exacto variará de familia en familia, pero el principio es el contacto constante y continuo — no una sola visita al principio seguida de años de silencio. Las familias de un diácono fiel saben de él a lo largo del año, en las buenas temporadas y en las malas, de modo que él está siempre a la mano.

blocks.en: It is worth saying that the ordinary, uneventful visit is the foundation of all the rest. A deacon who only appears in emergencies will always feel like a stranger when he comes; but one who has shared coffee and conversation in calmer days has earned the right to be present in the hard ones. The quiet visits, when nothing is wrong, are what make the urgent visits welcome.
blocks.es_reference: Vale la pena decir que la visita ordinaria y sin novedad es el fundamento de todo lo demás. Un diácono que solo aparece en las emergencias siempre se sentirá como un extraño cuando venga; pero el que ha compartido café y conversación en días más calmados se ha ganado el derecho de estar presente en los difíciles. Las visitas calladas, cuando nada anda mal, son las que hacen bienvenidas las visitas urgentes.

blocks.en: III. The Ministry of Visitation: How to Visit Well
blocks.es_reference: III. El Ministerio de la Visitación: Cómo Visitar Bien

blocks.en: A visit may be done well or poorly, and a few simple principles make the difference. The deacon goes warmly and humbly, as a servant and not as an inspector. The visit is about them, not about him; he comes to listen far more than to talk, to learn their needs and to know their hearts.
blocks.es_reference: Una visita puede hacerse bien o mal, y unos pocos principios sencillos hacen la diferencia. El diácono va cálida y humildemente, como un siervo y no como un inspector. La visita es acerca de ellos, no acerca de él; viene a escuchar mucho más que a hablar, a aprender sus necesidades y a conocer sus corazones.

blocks.en: Illustration. Often the greatest gift a visitor can bring is simply to be there. When Job's friends first came to him, they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights and said not a word, “for they saw that his grief was very great” (Job 2:13). In that silence they ministered well; it was only later, when they opened their mouths, that they went wrong. A deacon need not arrive with clever words or ready answers. His presence, his listening ear, and his quiet sympathy will often say far more than any speech.
blocks.es_reference: Ilustración. A menudo el mayor regalo que un visitante puede traer es sencillamente estar ahí. Cuando los amigos de Job vinieron a él por primera vez, se sentaron con él en tierra siete días y siete noches y no dijeron una palabra, «porque veían que su dolor era muy grande» (Job 2:13). En ese silencio ministraron bien; fue solo después, cuando abrieron la boca, que erraron. Un diácono no necesita llegar con palabras ingeniosas ni respuestas listas. Su presencia, su oído atento y su callada compasión dirán a menudo mucho más que cualquier discurso.

blocks.en: The deacon also brings the Lord into the visit. A word of Scripture and a prayer, fitted gently to the moment, turn a friendly call into a means of grace, for he comes not merely as a neighbor but as a servant of Christ. He guards confidentiality strictly: what is shared within the home stays there, a matter we will weigh more fully in Unit 8, for a deacon who carries tales destroys the very trust his ministry depends upon. He knows, too, when to leave; a visit need not be long, and an unhurried but not endless call is a blessing, while overstaying only wearies. And he avoids the common pitfalls — prying into what is not offered, filling the time with his own stories, or turning a family's sorrow into gossip afterward.
blocks.es_reference: El diácono también trae al Señor a la visita. Una palabra de la Escritura y una oración, ajustadas con suavidad al momento, convierten una visita amistosa en un medio de gracia, porque él viene no meramente como un vecino sino como un siervo de Cristo. Guarda estrictamente la confidencialidad: lo que se comparte dentro del hogar se queda ahí, un asunto que pesaremos más plenamente en la Unidad 8, porque un diácono que lleva cuentos destruye la confianza misma de la que depende su ministerio. Sabe, además, cuándo partir; una visita no necesita ser larga, y una visita sin prisa pero no interminable es una bendición, mientras que quedarse demasiado solo cansa. Y evita los errores comunes — husmear en lo que no se ofrece, llenar el tiempo con sus propias historias, o convertir la tristeza de una familia en chisme después.

blocks.en: One thing more sets a good visit apart: it does not end at the door. The deacon who notices a need carries it away with him — to pray over it, to mention it (with care) to the pastor, to return with help if help is needed. A visit that merely passes the time is pleasant; a visit that leads to real ministry is what the Plan is for.
blocks.es_reference: Una cosa más distingue a una buena visita: no termina en la puerta. El diácono que nota una necesidad se la lleva consigo — para orar por ella, para mencionarla (con cuidado) al pastor, para volver con ayuda si la ayuda hace falta. Una visita que meramente pasa el tiempo es agradable; una visita que conduce a un ministerio real es para lo que el Plan existe.

blocks.en: IV. The Ministry of Prayer
blocks.es_reference: IV. El Ministerio de la Oración

blocks.en: If visitation is the deacon's most visible work, prayer is his most powerful. Here he carries his families, one by one, into the presence of God. The deacon prays for his families by name; and to pray for them by name he must know them — their burdens, their sicknesses, their struggles and their joys — so that his prayer is specific and real and not a vague good wish. He prays with them as well: in the visit, at the bedside, in the hour of crisis, a prayer offered aloud brings the comfort and the power of God right into the room.
blocks.es_reference: Si la visitación es la obra más visible del diácono, la oración es la más poderosa. Aquí lleva a sus familias, una por una, a la presencia de Dios. El diácono ora por sus familias por nombre; y para orar por ellas por nombre debe conocerlas — sus cargas, sus enfermedades, sus luchas y sus gozos — de modo que su oración sea específica y real y no un vago buen deseo. Ora con ellas también: en la visita, junto a la cama, en la hora de crisis, una oración ofrecida en voz alta trae el consuelo y el poder de Dios justo a la habitación.

blocks.en: The priority of prayer stands very high. When the apostles appointed the seven, they reserved for themselves “prayer and the ministry of the word” (Acts 6:4) — and they named prayer first. Epaphras “always labored fervently” in prayers for his people (Colossians 4:12). And the prophet Samuel counted it a sin even to stop:
blocks.es_reference: La prioridad de la oración es muy alta. Cuando los apóstoles nombraron a los siete, reservaron para sí mismos «la oración y el ministerio de la palabra» (Hechos 6:4) — y nombraron la oración primero. Epafras «siempre trabajaba fervientemente» en oraciones por su pueblo (Colosenses 4:12). Y el profeta Samuel contó como pecado aun el dejar de hacerlo:

blocks.en: Moreover, as for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you; but I will teach you the good and the right way. (1 Samuel 12:23, NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: Así que, lejos sea de mí que peque yo contra Jehová cesando de rogar por vosotros; antes os enseñaré por el camino bueno y recto. (1 Samuel 12:23, RVG)

blocks.en: For the deacon, to cease praying for his families would be to fail them at the deepest level of all. He cannot always fix their troubles; but he can always pray, and very often the praying accomplishes more than any fixing could. Let no deacon think that prayer is the least he can do for his families. In truth it is the most.
blocks.es_reference: Para el diácono, cesar de orar por sus familias sería fallarles en el nivel más profundo de todos. No siempre puede arreglar sus dificultades; pero siempre puede orar, y muy a menudo el orar logra más de lo que cualquier arreglo podría. Que ningún diácono piense que la oración es lo menos que puede hacer por sus familias. En verdad es lo más.

blocks.en: The deacon's praying need not be solitary, either. As he learns the needs of his families, he can bring them — carefully, and only as far as is fitting — before the prayers of the other deacons and, where appropriate, the whole church, so that many hands are lifted for one burdened home. In this way the care of a single deacon opens into the intercession of the entire body.
blocks.es_reference: El orar del diácono tampoco tiene por qué ser solitario. Conforme aprende las necesidades de sus familias, puede llevarlas — con cuidado, y solo hasta donde sea apropiado — ante las oraciones de los otros diáconos y, donde convenga, de toda la iglesia, de modo que muchas manos se levanten por un solo hogar cargado. De esta manera el cuidado de un solo diácono se abre a la intercesión de todo el cuerpo.

blocks.en: V. Faithful Through the Years
blocks.es_reference: V. Fiel a Través de los Años

blocks.en: These two ministries are sustained by a single virtue: faithfulness. The danger to ongoing care is rarely a bad beginning; it is a slow fading — visits that grow rare, prayers that grow vague, until at last the family is forgotten again and the back door stands open once more.
blocks.es_reference: Estos dos ministerios son sostenidos por una sola virtud: la fidelidad. El peligro para el cuidado continuo rara vez es un mal comienzo; es un lento desvanecerse — visitas que se vuelven raras, oraciones que se vuelven vagas, hasta que por fin la familia es olvidada de nuevo y la puerta trasera queda abierta una vez más.

blocks.en: Faithfulness is what keeps the ministry alive: regular contact maintained, a simple record of visits and needs kept up as Unit 5 urged, and a steady refusal to grow weary in the work. “Let us not grow weary while doing good,” Paul wrote, “for in due season we shall reap if we do not lose heart” (Galatians 6:9). The reward of such faithfulness is a ministry that deepens over the years into a trusted bond — a deacon who has walked with his families through sickness and health, through birth and death, until they would think to call him first in any trouble. That is what ongoing care finally becomes.
blocks.es_reference: La fidelidad es lo que mantiene vivo el ministerio: el contacto regular mantenido, un sencillo registro de visitas y necesidades llevado al día como la Unidad 5 urgió, y una firme negativa a cansarse en la obra. «No nos cansemos, pues, de hacer bien,» escribió Pablo, «porque a su tiempo segaremos, si no desmayamos» (Gálatas 6:9). La recompensa de tal fidelidad es un ministerio que se profundiza con los años hasta convertirse en un vínculo de confianza — un diácono que ha caminado con sus familias por enfermedad y salud, por nacimiento y muerte, hasta que pensarían en llamarlo a él primero en cualquier dificultad. Eso es lo que el cuidado continuo finalmente llega a ser.

blocks.en: Much of this faithfulness goes unseen. No crowd applauds the deacon who drives across town on a cold night to sit with a dying saint, or who prays, year upon year, for a family that never knows it. But it is seen by the One who matters, who has promised that the cup of cold water given in His name will not lose its reward. The faithful deacon labors for an audience of One.
blocks.es_reference: Mucha de esta fidelidad pasa desapercibida. Ninguna multitud aplaude al diácono que cruza la ciudad en una noche fría para sentarse con un santo moribundo, o que ora, año tras año, por una familia que nunca lo sabe. Pero es visto por Aquel que importa, quien ha prometido que el vaso de agua fría dado en su nombre no perderá su recompensa. El diácono fiel trabaja para una audiencia de Uno.

blocks.en: Conclusion
blocks.es_reference: Conclusión

blocks.en: The introduction of Unit 5 only opened the door; ongoing care is the walking through it, again and again, year after year. The deacon goes to his families and he prays for his families, and he keeps doing both, faithfully, when it is convenient and when it is not. Everything else in the Plan rests upon this steady, unglamorous, Christlike work.
blocks.es_reference: La presentación de la Unidad 5 solo abrió la puerta; el cuidado continuo es el caminar a través de ella, una y otra vez, año tras año. El diácono va a sus familias y ora por sus familias, y sigue haciendo ambas cosas, fielmente, cuando es conveniente y cuando no lo es. Todo lo demás en el Plan descansa sobre esta obra constante, sin gloria, semejante a la de Cristo.

blocks.en: Programs may come and go, and methods may be improved, but nothing will ever replace a caring man at the door and a praying man on his knees. Where those two are found, the Plan is alive; where they are missing, no amount of organization can make up the lack.
blocks.es_reference: Los programas pueden ir y venir, y los métodos pueden mejorarse, pero nada reemplazará jamás a un hombre solícito en la puerta y a un hombre orando de rodillas. Donde esos dos se hallan, el Plan está vivo; donde faltan, ninguna cantidad de organización puede suplir la carencia.

blocks.en: “Pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this: to visit... in their trouble.” The deacon who faithfully visits and prays is practicing the purest kind of religion there is — the very care of Christ, carried to every home. With this rhythm of care established, we turn in Unit 7 to a deeper purpose hidden within it: how the deacon, even as he visits and prays, also disciples and evangelizes the families given into his care.
blocks.es_reference: «La religión pura y sin mácula delante de Dios y Padre es esta: Visitar... en sus tribulaciones.» El diácono que fielmente visita y ora está practicando la clase más pura de religión que existe — el cuidado mismo de Cristo, llevado a cada hogar. Con este ritmo de cuidado establecido, nos volvemos en la Unidad 7 a un propósito más profundo escondido dentro de él: cómo el diácono, aun mientras visita y ora, también discipula y evangeliza a las familias dadas a su cuidado.

sa.prompt: Why must the deacon's care be ongoing and not only in a crisis?
sa.model: The deacon's care must be ongoing because care that arrives only in a crisis is too little and too late. The relationship has to be kept alive between the troubles, so that when trouble finally comes the deacon is already a trusted friend and not a stranger knocking at the door. A man who only appears in emergencies will always feel like a stranger, but one who has visited in calmer days has earned the right to be present in the hard ones. The quiet, ordinary contact is the very foundation that makes the urgent ministry welcome.

sa.prompt: What are the two great ministries of ongoing care, and what does each one do?
sa.model: The two great ministries of ongoing care are visitation and prayer. By the ministry of visitation the deacon goes to his families where they are, being present with them in person; he visits the sick, the grieving, the absent, the new, and the lonely, and rejoices with them in their joys. By the ministry of prayer the deacon carries his families to God, praying for them by name and praying with them in their need. Together these two, sustained by faithfulness, are how the deacon actually cares for the families entrusted to him.

sa.prompt: Show from Scripture why visitation is a biblical ministry.
sa.model: Visitation is a thoroughly biblical ministry. James calls it the heart of pure religion, to visit the orphan and the widow in their trouble. The Lord Himself, in Matthew 25, counts visiting the sick and the imprisoned as done unto Him, for whatever is done to the least of His brethren is done to Christ. Paul followed this pattern, teaching not only publicly but from house to house, in Acts 20:20. And it follows the way of God, who did not merely send a message but sent His Son to dwell among us. So the deacon visits because his Lord first came.

sa.prompt: Whom does the deacon visit, and how often?
sa.model: The deacon visits all of his families, since the whole point of the Plan is that every family has ongoing contact and not only the few who speak up. Beyond that regular contact, he gives special and prompt attention to those in particular need: the sick and the shut-in, who cannot come to the church; the bereaved in their grief; the absent and the drifting, before the back door closes; the new and the lonely; and he comes in times of joy as well. As for how often, he visits regularly enough that the relationship stays alive, in good seasons and bad.

sa.prompt: Describe how to visit well (the manner of a good visit).
sa.model: To visit well, the deacon goes warmly and humbly, as a servant and not as an inspector. The visit is about the family, not about him, so he listens far more than he talks, seeking to learn their needs and know their hearts. Often his greatest gift is simply to be present, for his quiet sympathy says more than clever words. He brings the Lord into the visit with a word of Scripture and a prayer; he guards confidentiality strictly; he knows when to leave, never overstaying; and he avoids prying, dominating with his own stories, or repeating a family's sorrow as gossip afterward.

sa.prompt: Explain the ministry of prayer for the deacon's families.
sa.model: The ministry of prayer is the deacon carrying his families, one by one, into the presence of God. He prays for them by name, and to do so he must truly know them, their burdens, sicknesses, struggles, and joys, so that his prayer is specific and real rather than a vague good wish. He also prays with them, at the bedside and in the hour of crisis, where a prayer offered aloud brings the comfort and power of God into the room. As he learns their needs, he may also bring them, carefully, before the prayers of the other deacons and the whole church.

sa.prompt: Why is prayer called the deacon's most powerful work, not the least?
sa.model: Prayer is called the deacon's most powerful work, not the least, because while he cannot always fix his families' troubles, he can always pray, and very often the praying accomplishes more than any fixing could. The priority of prayer stands high in Scripture: the apostles named prayer first when they reserved prayer and the word for themselves, Epaphras labored fervently in prayer for his people, and Samuel called it a sin even to cease praying. To stop praying for his families would be to fail them at the deepest level of all. So no deacon should think prayer is the least he can do; it is the most.

sa.prompt: What does Job 2:13 teach about the ministry of presence?
sa.model: Job 2:13 teaches the ministry of presence. When Job's friends first came to him, they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights and said not a word, because they saw that his grief was very great. In that silence they ministered well; it was only later, when they opened their mouths, that they went wrong. The lesson for the deacon is that he need not arrive with clever words or ready answers. Often his presence, his listening ear, and his quiet sympathy say far more than any speech, and simply being there is the greatest gift.

sa.prompt: Why is faithfulness the virtue that sustains ongoing care?
sa.model: Faithfulness is the virtue that sustains ongoing care because the danger is rarely a bad beginning; it is a slow fading. Visits grow rare, prayers grow vague, and at last the family is forgotten again and the back door stands open once more. Faithfulness keeps the ministry alive by maintaining regular contact, keeping a simple record of visits and needs, and refusing to grow weary, for Paul said we shall reap in due season if we do not lose heart. Much of this labor is unseen by people, but it is seen by God, and the faithful deacon works for an audience of One.

sa.prompt: Summarize the deacon's ministry of ongoing care.
sa.model: The deacon's ministry of ongoing care is the steady, year-round work by which he actually cares for his families, and it flows through two great ministries held up by faithfulness. By visitation he goes to them in person, visiting the sick, the grieving, the absent, and the lonely, and rejoicing in their joys. By prayer he carries them to God, interceding for them by name and praying with them in their need. And by faithfulness he keeps both alive through the years, refusing to let the care fade. This humble, Christlike work is the foundation on which the whole Plan rests.
